lines.text: Lesson 1 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/01_production_contract.py
Why this matters
A pipeline that works once is a prototype. Production engineering begins when the same result must stay correct
through retries, source changes, expired credentials, deployments, and downstream expectations. Your job is no
longer just to make code run; it is to define the promise, collect evidence that the promise is being met, and recover
safely when it is not.
Picture it in your head
Picture a restaurant kitchen serving 300 customers. Good cooking is necessary, but production also needs order
tickets, food-safety checks, handoffs, inventory, ownership, and a recovery plan. A data pipeline is similar:
transformation code is only one station in a larger operating system.
New words before we use them

rows: A written statement of correctness, freshness, security and recovery promises.
A measurable reliability target such as freshness or success rate.
How much data or business behavior one failure can affect.
A tested operational procedure for a known failure class.
The ability to restore a correct state without inventing or losing accepted data.

Use rule: Watch/read for the mental model or current interface, then return to this learner book and supplied practice.
External media never replaces the independent task or validation evidence.
Follow with me once
Take a nightly orders pipeline. Write five promises before choosing tools: every accepted order appears once in
curated data; paid revenue reconciles to source; data is ready by 06:00; secrets never appear in code/logs; and a
bad release can be rolled back without deleting accepted source evidence. Map each promise to one independent
proof. A green scheduler icon is not one of those proofs.
What you should see / why it worked
You should finish with a small production contract where another engineer can tell what healthy means, where to look
for evidence, and which failure should stop publication. The reason this works is that the control is explicit,
measurable and separated from hidden assumptions. A trustworthy result is not merely an output; it includes the
boundary that was checked and evidence that can be reviewed later.
Break it: a realistic failure
At 05:40 the orchestration UI says success, but the gold table contains only 12% of the normal rows because the
source API changed pagination. Compute succeeded; the business contract failed. A row-count/reconciliation gate
must stop publication and preserve the previous good state.
Reason through the incident
Work in this order: 1) preserve the failing evidence; 2) identify which contract or boundary failed; 3) bound blast
radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.
Now you do a changed version alone
Create a production contract for a daily customer-status pipeline. Include correctness, freshness, access, deployment
and recovery promises. Name one owner and one evidence source for each promise.
Fresh changed retry
Change the case to a streaming payments feed. Decide which promises need tighter latency, what
replay/deduplication evidence is required, and what can remain eventually consistent.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when the required output and the named control both agree; a green command alone is insufficient.
• If the result is PARTIAL, first inspect inputs/configuration/permissions, then reproduce the smallest failing case.
• Never repair by deleting evidence or by granting broad privilege just to make an error disappear.
• After repair, change the fixture or scenario and prove the same principle still holds under a fresh case.
Ready-made revision
Core idea: Production mindset is about making production behavior explicit, reviewable and recoverable. The
learner should be able to state the contract, show evidence, describe a failure boundary and perform a changed retry
without copying the demonstration.
Teach it back
Explain why 'the DAG is green' is not enough to call a data product healthy. Give two examples of successful
execution with wrong business output.
Evidence / mastery
Save: the genuine first attempt, any error/failure output, the corrected result, one validation proof, and a short
explanation of why the control protects production. Do not overwrite the first failed evidence with the repaired run.
Lesson 2 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/02_test_strategy.py
Why this matters
Data systems fail at many layers: a pure function can be wrong, a schema can drift, a database boundary can
misbehave, a join can change grain, or totals can stop reconciling. One enormous end-to-end test is slow and hard to
diagnose; only unit tests are too narrow. A useful strategy layers evidence by defect class.
Picture it in your head
Think of airport security. Identity, luggage, boarding eligibility and aircraft safety are separate checkpoints. No single
checkpoint proves everything. Data testing needs the same defense-in-depth idea.
New words before we use them

rows: A fast check of small deterministic logic.
A check across a real component boundary.
A check that an interface still has expected schema or semantics.
An independent comparison of counts, keys or business measures across stages.
Small controlled input used to make a test reproducible.

Follow with me once
For order totals, first test the pure aggregation function with three rows. Then check required columns/types and
non-null business keys. Next write the result to a disposable database. Finally reconcile source quantity*price against
the curated sum. Each layer should tell you what class of defect it can catch and what it cannot prove.
What you should see / why it worked
A test matrix that names the test layer, fixture, command, expected result, runtime/cost, and defect class. Fast tests
belong on every pull request; expensive environment checks belong at stronger release boundaries. The reason this
works is that the control is explicit, measurable and separated from hidden assumptions. A trustworthy result is not
merely an output; it includes the boundary that was checked and evidence that can be reviewed later.
Break it: a realistic failure
A refactor passes 65 unit tests but doubles daily revenue because a join changed grain and created fan-out. The
missing proof was not another helper-function test; it was a grain/reconciliation assertion at the data boundary.
Reason through the incident
Work in this order: 1) preserve the failing evidence; 2) identify which contract or boundary failed; 3) bound blast
radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.
Now you do a changed version alone
Build an eight-test matrix for ingestion -> staging -> curated. Use at least four layers and mark which tests run on
every pull request versus before production promotion.
Fresh changed retry
The source adds nullable coupon_code. Decide what should continue to pass, what would fail if the field became
required, and how backwards compatibility is demonstrated.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when the required output and the named control both agree; a green command alone is insufficient.
• If the result is PARTIAL, first inspect inputs/configuration/permissions, then reproduce the smallest failing case.
• Never repair by deleting evidence or by granting broad privilege just to make an error disappear.
• After repair, change the fixture or scenario and prove the same principle still holds under a fresh case.
Ready-made revision
Core idea: Testing strategy for data engineering is about making production behavior explicit, reviewable and
recoverable. The learner should be able to state the contract, show evidence, describe a failure boundary and
perform a changed retry without copying the demonstration.
Teach it back
Using one orders example, distinguish a unit test, a data-quality expectation, an integration test and a reconciliation
check.
Evidence / mastery
Save: the genuine first attempt, any error/failure output, the corrected result, one validation proof, and a short
explanation of why the control protects production. Do not overwrite the first failed evidence with the repaired run.
Lesson 3 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/03_quality_gate.py
Why this matters
A validation report becomes operationally useful only when its result controls a decision. A quality gate turns
measurements into pass, warn, quarantine or fail-closed behavior so technically processed but unfit data cannot
quietly reach consumers.
Picture it in your head
A railway signal does not repair the track; it prevents a train from entering an unsafe block. A data quality gate does
the same at a publish or deploy boundary.
New words before we use them

rows: A decision point that blocks or routes work based on explicit validation rules.
A violation that stops publication or deployment.
A recorded anomaly that does not block the flow.
A safe retained location/state for rejected evidence.
A measurable boundary such as null-rate <= 0.5%.

Follow with me once
For a customer batch define four rules: non-empty; customer_id unique/non-null; country in allowed set; row count at
least 80% of rolling baseline. Run a good fixture and then a duplicate-ID fixture. The gate must emit
machine-readable evidence, refuse publication on the hard failure, and retain the rejected batch for diagnosis.
What you should see / why it worked
A result containing rule name, measured value, threshold, severity and final decision. On a hard failure the committed
accepted checkpoint must remain unchanged. The reason this works is that the control is explicit, measurable and
separated from hidden assumptions. A trustworthy result is not merely an output; it includes the boundary that was
checked and evidence that can be reviewed later.
Break it: a realistic failure
A source sends half the normal rows after an upstream timeout. Schema and uniqueness pass, but volume fails. If
you advance the checkpoint before validation, replay becomes harder and bad progress is now accepted state.
Correct behavior is quarantine + alert + no publish + no checkpoint advance.
Reason through the incident
Work in this order: 1) preserve the failing evidence; 2) identify which contract or boundary failed; 3) bound blast
radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.
Now you do a changed version alone
Add a paid-revenue reconciliation rule and a freshness rule. Make one warning-only and one blocking, then justify the
business consequence behind each severity.
Fresh changed retry
Change the volume baseline by 20% and show why the same incoming batch changes decision only because the
contractual threshold changed. Record the rule version.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when the required output and the named control both agree; a green command alone is insufficient.
• If the result is PARTIAL, first inspect inputs/configuration/permissions, then reproduce the smallest failing case.
• Never repair by deleting evidence or by granting broad privilege just to make an error disappear.
• After repair, change the fixture or scenario and prove the same principle still holds under a fresh case.
Ready-made revision
Core idea: Automated quality gates is about making production behavior explicit, reviewable and recoverable. The
learner should be able to state the contract, show evidence, describe a failure boundary and perform a changed retry
without copying the demonstration.
Teach it back
Why is a validation report alone not a quality gate? Name the additional control that makes it a gate.
Evidence / mastery
Save: the genuine first attempt, any error/failure output, the corrected result, one validation proof, and a short
explanation of why the control protects production. Do not overwrite the first failed evidence with the repaired run.
Lesson 4 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/04_ci_simulator.py
Why this matters
Continuous Integration (CI) means small changes are integrated frequently and checked automatically before they
damage the shared codebase. For data projects, CI can compile Python, run deterministic tests, validate
SQL/configuration, check fixture-based contracts and scan for obvious secret leakage without needing production
access.
Picture it in your head
Imagine a bridge inspected after each small repair rather than after six months of unreviewed changes. CI does not
guarantee safe production, but it finds cheap defects while the change is still small and attributable.
New words before we use them

rows: An automated sequence triggered by repository events.
The machine that executes CI jobs.
A set of steps executed in one runner context.
A file produced by the workflow, such as a test report.
Automated evidence attached to a proposed change before merge.

Follow with me once
Declare a minimal flow: checkout -> set up Python -> install locked dependencies -> compile -> unit tests -> fixture
quality checks -> secret-pattern scan. Deliberately fail unit tests. The simulator should prove that later release steps
are unreachable, then identify the failed stage in the evidence.
What you should see / why it worked
Every required check either passes or stops the workflow with a non-zero decision. A reviewer can see which gate
failed without rerunning your laptop setup. The reason this works is that the control is explicit, measurable and
separated from hidden assumptions. A trustworthy result is not merely an output; it includes the boundary that was
checked and evidence that can be reviewed later.
Break it: a realistic failure
Common mistakes are running CI only after merge, hiding errors with continue-on-error, using floating dependencies,
or putting powerful production credentials into a test workflow that never needed them. Workflow files themselves are
executable code and must be reviewed as a trust boundary.
Reason through the incident
Work in this order: 1) preserve the failing evidence; 2) identify which contract or boundary failed; 3) bound blast
radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.
Now you do a changed version alone
Write a CI matrix for the M16 practice repository: trigger, job, command, expected artifact and failure effect. Include at
least one check requiring no network.
Fresh changed retry
First make the unit-test stage fail and prove deploy is unreachable. Then fix it and introduce a secret-pattern failure
so a different gate blocks the path.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when the required output and the named control both agree; a green command alone is insufficient.
• If the result is PARTIAL, first inspect inputs/configuration/permissions, then reproduce the smallest failing case.
• Never repair by deleting evidence or by granting broad privilege just to make an error disappear.
• After repair, change the fixture or scenario and prove the same principle still holds under a fresh case.
Ready-made revision
Core idea: Continuous Integration fundamentals is about making production behavior explicit, reviewable and
recoverable. The learner should be able to state the contract, show evidence, describe a failure boundary and
perform a changed retry without copying the demonstration.
Teach it back
Explain CI to someone who believes it means 'automatically deploy every commit.' What is missing from that
definition?

Save: the genuine first attempt, any error/failure output, the corrected result, one validation proof, and a short
explanation of why the control protects production. Do not overwrite the first failed evidence with the repaired run.
Lesson 5 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/05_github_actions_ci.yml
Why this matters
GitHub Actions is one practical CI/CD engine for repository events. The important skill is not memorizing YAML; it is
understanding event -> job -> runner -> step -> permissions -> evidence so you can reason about what executes and
what authority it has.
Picture it in your head
Think of a factory work order. The event opens the work order, the job is a station, the runner is the workstation, steps
are operations, and permissions decide which locked cabinets that station may open.
New words before we use them

rows: Repository activity that can trigger a workflow.
Executes shell commands on the runner.
Short-lived token scoped to the workflow/repository.
Federated identity mechanism that can avoid storing long-lived cloud credentials.

Follow with me once
Read the supplied workflow. It runs on pull_request and manual workflow_dispatch, grants contents: read, checks out
code, sets up Python, compiles the practice folder and runs the quality gate. Notice that test CI needs no production
secret. Then inspect where permissions are declared and why adding write-all would increase blast radius.
name: m16-ci
on:
pull_request:
workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
contents: read
jobs:
validate:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v6
- uses: actions/setup-python@v5
with:
python-version: '3.13'
- run: python -m compileall 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns
- run: python 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/03_quality_gate.py
What you should see / why it worked
You can identify trigger, job, runner image, reusable actions, shell commands, permissions and fail-closed checks.
You can also explain which steps could run safely on an untrusted pull request. The reason this works is that the
control is explicit, measurable and separated from hidden assumptions. A trustworthy result is not merely an output; it
includes the boundary that was checked and evidence that can be reviewed later.
Break it: a realistic failure
A workflow uses a long-lived cloud key stored as a secret even though the provider supports OIDC. The key is copied
into a debug command and appears in logs. The correct design is to remove unnecessary privilege, rotate/revoke
leaked credentials, and prefer short-lived federated identity with explicit trust conditions.
Reason through the incident
Work in this order: 1) preserve the failing evidence; 2) identify which contract or boundary failed; 3) bound blast
radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.
Now you do a changed version alone
Create a branch-safe workflow that compiles code and runs two deterministic checks. Keep permissions read-only.
Describe what additional controls would be required before adding deployment.
Fresh changed retry
Add a second job that depends on validate and produces a harmless text artifact. Break validate and prove the
artifact job does not run; then repair it.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when the required output and the named control both agree; a green command alone is insufficient.
• If the result is PARTIAL, first inspect inputs/configuration/permissions, then reproduce the smallest failing case.
• Never repair by deleting evidence or by granting broad privilege just to make an error disappear.
• After repair, change the fixture or scenario and prove the same principle still holds under a fresh case.
Ready-made revision
Core idea: GitHub Actions for data projects is about making production behavior explicit, reviewable and
recoverable. The learner should be able to state the contract, show evidence, describe a failure boundary and
perform a changed retry without copying the demonstration.
Teach it back
What is the difference between `uses:` and `run:`? Why should workflow permissions be designed explicitly?

explanation of why the control protects production. Do not overwrite the first failed evidence with the repaired run.
Lesson 6 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/06_environment_binding.py
Why this matters
Environment separation limits blast radius and makes promotion reviewable. The goal is not three unrelated copies of
a platform; it is the same tested artifact bound to different data, identities, endpoints and capacity according to
environment policy.
Picture it in your head
Picture the same train model running first on a test track, then on a restricted certification track, then on the main
network. The train design should not silently change between tracks; the track bindings and permissions do.
New words before we use them

rows: A controlled execution boundary such as dev, test or prod.
Values that vary without changing application logic.
Moving a tested version to a more trusted environment.
Unreviewed difference between intended and actual environment settings.
Connection from an artifact to environment-specific resources.

Follow with me once
Use one pipeline artifact and three configuration maps. Dev reads synthetic/local data, test reads a controlled
integration source, prod reads the approved production source. The binding checker rejects a configuration where the
test artifact points at the production customer table. This is environment safety expressed as code.
What you should see / why it worked
You can show the same artifact/version across environments while endpoints, identities and capacities change

the boundary that was checked and evidence that can be reviewed later.

A test pipeline is copied manually from production and still references the prod sink. A harmless test run overwrites
business data. The root cause is not 'someone clicked wrong'; it is missing environment binding controls and
excessive test identity permissions.

Work in this order: 1) preserve the failing evidence; 2) identify which contract or boundary failed; 3) bound blast
radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.

data-sensitivity differences.

Lesson 7 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/07_deploy_rollback_simulator.py
Why this matters
Deployment changes running behavior; rollback is the controlled path back when a release proves unsafe. Data
engineering adds a complication: rolling code back does not automatically undo data that the bad code already wrote.
Release design must separate code rollback, data repair and replay.
Picture it in your head
Imagine replacing a machine on an assembly line. You can reinstall the old machine, but defective products already
produced do not disappear. They need identification, quarantine and reprocessing.
New words before we use them

rows: Promotion of a version/configuration into an environment.
Returning code/configuration to a previously known-good version.
Fixing by deploying a new corrected version.
A controlled change to stored schema/state.
Compatibility pattern that introduces changes before removing old behavior.

the boundary that was checked and evidence that can be reviewed later.

A destructive schema migration drops a column before all consumers are updated. Rolling application code back
cannot recreate the deleted values. Safer changes often use expand-contract: add compatible structure,
migrate/verify readers, then remove old structure in a later controlled release.

radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.

Write a release checklist for a pipeline with a Delta table and one downstream dashboard. Include pre-deploy
evidence, smoke/reconciliation checks and data-repair decision points.

Change the case so v2 writes an idempotent derived table rather than destructive state. Explain why replay is now
easier and what evidence still matters.

• PASS only when the required output and the named control both agree; a green command alone is insufficient.
• If the result is PARTIAL, first inspect inputs/configuration/permissions, then reproduce the smallest failing case.

Lesson 8 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/08_secret_hygiene.py
Why this matters
Credentials are authority. A leaked secret is not just untidy text; it can let an attacker or accidental process act as
your system. Modern cloud workflows therefore prefer managed identities or short-lived federation such as OIDC
over copied long-lived keys whenever the platform supports it.
Picture it in your head
A password written on a sticky note is dangerous because anyone who sees it inherits your authority. A managed
identity is closer to a guarded badge issued to a known workload for a limited purpose and lifetime.
New words before we use them

rows: Sensitive authentication material such as token, key or password.
Cloud identity assigned to a workload instead of embedding credentials.
Trust exchange that can issue short-lived provider credentials based on workflow identity.
Replacing credential material and invalidating the old value.
Rule restricting which identity claims are allowed to obtain credentials.

Use rule: Watch/read for the mental model or current interface, then return to this learner book and supplied practice.
External media never replaces the independent task or validation evidence.
Follow with me once
Run the hygiene scanner over sample configuration. It should flag obvious embedded tokens but not treat the
scanner as complete protection. Then sketch a GitHub Actions -> cloud OIDC flow: workflow identity token, cloud
trust policy, short-lived role/session, least-privilege access. No long-lived cloud key is committed to the repository.
What you should see / why it worked
You can explain where secret material may leak (code, git history, logs, notebooks, config exports) and what to do
after exposure: revoke/rotate, investigate use, remove from future code/history where appropriate, and replace the
design. The reason this works is that the control is explicit, measurable and separated from hidden assumptions. A
trustworthy result is not merely an output; it includes the boundary that was checked and evidence that can be
reviewed later.
Break it: a realistic failure
A key is accidentally committed and then 'fixed' by deleting the line in the next commit. The key still exists in history
and may already have been copied. Treat it as compromised immediately; revoke/rotate first. Cleanup is secondary
to removing authority.
Reason through the incident
Work in this order: 1) preserve the failing evidence; 2) identify which contract or boundary failed; 3) bound blast
radius before changing state; 4) choose the smallest reversible repair; 5) rerun an independent validation; 6) record
what would prevent recurrence. If you skip evidence and jump straight to a fix, you may restore the dashboard while
losing the ability to explain why it failed.
Now you do a changed version alone
Take a hypothetical CI workflow currently using AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET. Redesign it around OIDC/managed
identity if supported. List trust conditions and least-privilege permissions.
Fresh changed retry
Assume OIDC is temporarily unavailable for one legacy service. Design a contained secret fallback with rotation,
restricted scope, masked logs and an explicit removal date.
Validation and recovery ladder
• PASS only when the required output and the named control both agree; a green command alone is insufficient.
• If the result is PARTIAL, first inspect inputs/configuration/permissions, then reproduce the smallest failing case.
• Never repair by deleting evidence or by granting broad privilege just to make an error disappear.

retry without copying the demonstration.

Lesson 9 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/09_rbac_least_privilege.py
Why this matters
Role-based access control (RBAC) limits who can do what at which scope. Least privilege means granting only the
actions and resource scope needed for the task, then reviewing access as responsibilities change. It reduces the
blast radius of mistakes and stolen identities.
Picture it in your head
In a hotel, a guest key opens one room for a time; housekeeping keys open assigned rooms; a master key is rare and
audited. Giving every employee the master key is convenient until the first mistake or loss.
New words before we use them

rows: User, group, service principal or managed identity receiving access.
Resource boundary where the assignment applies.
Operations that configure/manage the resource itself.

Lesson 10 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/10_pii_masking.py
Why this matters
Personal data creates a different risk class. Protecting it requires knowing where it exists, minimizing unnecessary
copies, encrypting storage and transport, controlling access, and ensuring logs/test fixtures/analytics do not expose
raw identifiers without a business need.
Picture it in your head
A hospital does not post patient charts in the hallway merely because the building door is locked. Storage encryption
is one layer; who can view which field and where copies appear is another.
New words before we use them

rows: Personally identifiable information that can identify or be linked to a person.
Protection of stored bytes using cryptographic keys.
Protection while data moves across networks.
Showing a transformed/redacted representation instead of raw sensitive value.
Keeping only data needed for the defined purpose.

Lesson 11 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/11_lineage_graph.py
Why this matters
When a field is wrong, teams need to know where it came from, what transformed it, who owns it, what consumes it
and whether it is sensitive. Metadata and lineage turn a collection of tables into an explainable data system and make
change impact review possible.
Picture it in your head
Imagine a subway map. A station name alone is useful, but the lines show how stations connect, where transfers
happen and what downstream routes are affected by a closure. Lineage is that connectivity map for data assets.
New words before we use them

rows: Information describing a data asset, such as owner, schema, grain or sensitivity.
Recorded upstream/downstream relationships between assets and transformations.
Policies, roles and processes for trustworthy and appropriate data use.
Searchable inventory of data assets and metadata.
Reasoning about what downstream assets may be affected by a change.

Lesson 12 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/12_observability_metrics.py
Why this matters
Monitoring tells you that a metric crossed a threshold; observability helps you understand system state from
evidence. Data pipelines need ordinary software signals plus data-specific signals such as freshness, volume,
schema, reconciliation and distribution because compute can look healthy while the data is wrong.
Picture it in your head
A car dashboard can show engine temperature and fuel, but if you are transporting medicine you also need cargo
temperature. Data systems likewise need infrastructure telemetry and data-product telemetry.
New words before we use them

rows: How current a dataset is relative to expectation.
Evidence about data health across freshness, volume, schema, quality and lineage/context.

Lesson 13 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/13_incident_rca.py
Why this matters
Production incidents are time-constrained reasoning problems. The goal is first to protect consumers and restore a
correct service, then to understand causes and strengthen the system. Good incident handling separates facts from
hypotheses and preserves evidence instead of improvising irreversible fixes.
Picture it in your head
Firefighters first contain the fire and protect people; the detailed origin investigation follows after the scene is safe.
Data incidents need the same separation between containment/recovery and root-cause analysis.
New words before we use them

rows: Unplanned event that degrades correctness, availability, security or service expectations.
Action limiting further harm before full cause is known.
Pre-tested operational steps for a known symptom/failure class.
Root-cause analysis explaining causal chain and prevention actions.
Possible explanation not yet proven by evidence.

Lesson 14 of 14 | Primary practice: 15_M16/practice/dataops_patterns/14_terraform_policy_check.py
Why this matters
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) expresses infrastructure intent in versioned files so changes can be reviewed, repeated
and compared rather than reconstructed from memory and portal clicks. Terraform is one widely used IaC tool. For
this course the stable baseline is Terraform 1.16.x; do not build the lesson around prerelease 1.17 behavior.
Picture it in your head
Think of a building blueprint plus change history. The blueprint does not physically construct the building by itself, but
it gives reviewers an explicit desired design and a repeatable basis for changes.

rows: Managing infrastructure configuration through versioned declarative code.
